caller.voice: Her flatmate, panicking and talking fast, in casual Singapore English. She knows only what she has seen: her flatmate is 24 and became breathless suddenly while clearing the dusty storeroom (the flat is under renovation), with a wheezing sound. She has had asthma since young, and her inhaler is empty.

answers.whatHappened: My flatmate, 24. Our flat renovating, she was clearing the storeroom, very dusty. Then suddenly she cannot breathe, got wheezing sound. She got asthma since young, but her inhaler empty already.
answers.conscious: Conscious, she can talk, but very breathless.
answers.icAndMeds: OK, I get her IC ready. Her inhaler empty already, but I keep it for you.
answers.breathing: Yes, breathing, but very fast, and got wheezing sound.

patient.name: Goh Hui Min
patient.voice: Breathless and wheezy. Speaks in full sentences, but stops for breath after each one.
patient.chiefComplaint: I suddenly can't breathe. It started when I was clearing the storeroom.

lines.feelingNow: A bit better with the oxygen. Still wheezy, still a bit breathless.
lines.hitHead: No, I didn't hit my head.
lines.neckPain: No, my neck is fine, no pain.
lines.lungHistory: Yes, I've had asthma since young. My inhaler is empty.
lines.verbal: Goh Hui Min. I'm at home, in Tampines.
lines.motor: OK, both arms up, like this.
lines.severity: 7. I really can't catch my breath.
lines.position: I'll stay sitting like this, leaning forward on the chair. It's easier.
lines.bpScreen: No shunt, no fistula. Never had any operation.
lines.ic: My IC is in my pocket, here.

hazards: renovation tools on the floor beside the patient

spine.dtbl: No deformities, tenderness, bruises or lacerations

circulation.pulse: Radial pulse present, fast and strong

investigation.auscultation: Air entry equal, expiratory wheeze both sides

position.choice: Sitting, leaning forward on a chair

oxygen.note: Asthma in respiratory distress gets salbutamol through a nebuliser mask at 6–8 L/min: salbutamol 2 ml with N/S 0.9% 2 ml, one dose only (notes 5, protocol 4; notes 16, Asthma: 'Management: inhaler or nebuliser'). Her asthma history means the 'no history of asthma or COPD' contraindication does not apply. Her SpO2 is 91%, under 95%, so she needs oxygen, with the device picked by her condition (notes 11). No signs of impending respiratory failure here: she speaks in full sentences, air entry is equal, she is alert and oriented, there is no cyanosis, and RR is 28.
